items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used to explain concepts, support research, and provide individualized learning assistance. Its growing presence raises questions about independent reasoning, creativity, verification, and equitable access. This exploratory cross-sectional survey examined respondents? reported AI use, perceived educational benefits, and cognitive abilities they considered important to protect. A total of 66 respondents participated in this exploratory cross-sectional survey, which combined descriptive quantitative analysis with summaries of open-ended responses. Sixty-four respondents (97.0%) reported using ChatGPT or a similar AI assistant. Personalized learning was selected as an expected benefit by 50 (75.8%), while 48 (72.7%) identified understanding difficult concepts as an AI use or benefit. Critical thinking was the most frequently selected cognitive skill to protect (55; 83.3%), followed by creativity (52; 78.8%), problem-solving (48; 72.7%), and decision-making (47; 71.2%). Reported themes included individualized explanations, convenient information access, dependence concerns, verification, equity, and teacher guidance. Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

items.abstract_text: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant growth in its integration with the field of Education. This has started many concerns about the effect it has on the process of learning, academic integrity and skill development. This paper examines the effects of AI use within the context of higher education institutions, as it investigates Moroccan postgraduate students’ perceptions on their academic achievements. The targeted sample consisted of 15 postgraduate students enrolled in the English departments of two public universities. This research follows a qualitative approach, as it aims to capture the students’ experience of AI use in their academic life. The findings highlight potential risks of heavy reliance on AI, which include a diminished confidence in the students’ performance, reduced engagement in independent learning and more. However, AI also presents many opportunities for enhancing the process of learning and education when used as a complementary tool instead of replacing the whole cognitive process. This study puts an emphasis on the need for a balanced AI integration while focusing on the development of the students’ cognitive skills in the process. This study contributes to the persisting debate regarding the implementation of AI tools in education and examines how they can be used ethically without diminishing students’ efforts or undermining their original contributions.

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, helping learners use AI effectively to solve language-related problems while maintaining independent judgment and critical thinking has become a key issue in technologyenhanced language education. However, existing studies have largely focused on EFL learners’ acceptance of AI, intentions to use it, and usage behaviors, offering limited explanations of how AI literacy shapes learners’ interactions with AI and relates to critical thinking. To address this gap, the present study drew on self-regulated learning theory and adopted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Questionnaire data from 450 university students with generative AIassisted EFL learning experience were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Subsequently, 20 participants selected through stratified purposive sampling took part in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically. Quantitative results showed that AI literacy was positively associated with AI-assisted problem-solving ability and indirectly associated with critical thinking through AI-assisted problem-solving ability and AI reliance. Thematic analysis further revealed how learners translated AI-related knowledge and skills into effective problem-solving practices and how different levels of cognitive control were associated with distinct patterns of AI use and cognitive outcomes. This study deepens the understanding of the internal cognitive mechanisms underlying EFL learners’ adaptation to AI and provides practical implications for the systematic development of AI literacy and critical thinking in EFL education.

items.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
items.preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
items.abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

items.abstract_text: This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. items.preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p &lt; .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p &lt; .001) and PU (β = .218, p &lt; .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p &lt; .001) and SRL (β = .202, p &lt; .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. Not applicable.

items.abstract_text: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. Our two-phase protocol first builds a category-balanced conversation corpus via PAIR-style iterative prompt refinement over API, then has trained human agents replay/refine those prompts in the consumer UI using a designated child account while monitoring the linked parent inbox for alerts. We focus on seven risk areas—physical harm, pornography, privacy violence, health consultation, fraud, hate speech, and malware—and quantify four outcomes: Notification Rate (NR), Leak-Through (LR), Overblocking (OBR), and UI Intervention Rate (UIR). Using an automated judge (with targeted human audit) and comparing the current backend to legacy variants (GPT-4.1/4o), we find that notifications are selective rather than comprehensive: privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, and malware triggered no parental alerts in our runs, whereas physical harm (highest), pornography, and some health queries produced intermittent alerts. The current backend shows lower leak-through than legacy models, yet overblocking of benign, educational queries near sensitive topics remains common and is not surfaced to parents, revealing a policy–product gap between on-screen safeguards and parent-facing telemetry. We propose actionable fixes: broaden/configure the notification taxonomy, couple visible safeguards to privacy-preserving parent summaries, and prefer calibrated, age-appropriate safe rewrites over blanket refusals.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

items.abstract_text: In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

items.abstract_text: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. This paper develops a conceptual model of how AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring reshapes psychological safety, the shared belief that a work environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking on which voice, dissent and error reporting depend. Integrating psychological-safety theory, the algorithmic-management and workplace-surveillance literatures, and organisational voice research, the paper argues that wellbeing-monitoring intensity depresses psychological safety principally through a mediating perception of surveillance threat, and that this relationship is not fixed but is conditioned by the transparency of the monitoring system, the degree to which employees attribute developmental rather than punitive intent to it, and whether a human manager mediates between algorithmic output and managerial action. Five propositions specify these relationships, including a boundary condition for India's IT-BPM sector, where the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 supplies a general consent-and-purpose-limitation framework but no sector-specific rule for wellbeing analytics, leaving adoption norms to be set informally inside a high-attrition, always-on operating environment. The paper closes with implications for the design of psychologically safe monitoring architectures and an agenda for empirical validation.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has diffused through higher education faster than the structures meant to govern it, yet acceptance research still treats adoption as a terminal outcome rather than as an event embedded in students&#39; self-regulation. This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by specifying metacognitive awareness (META) and self-regulated learning (SRL) as mediators between the four UTAUT determinants and behavioural intention (BI), and BI predicts self-reported use of GenAI as a cognitive partner (AU). Responses from 451 students at seven Thai Rajabhat universities were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM; SmartPLS 4; 10,000 bootstrap subsamples). Internal consistency was very high (above .95 for six of eight constructs), indicating partial item redundancy, and discriminant validity was supported under HTMT.90. Facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, showed the strongest associations with META (&beta; = .595) and SRL (&beta; = .514) but no significant direct association with intention (&beta; = .061, p = .430); their only significant indirect association with intention ran through META (&beta; = .186), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. Social influence was the strongest direct predictor of intention (&beta; = .357), followed by META (&beta; = .312); effort expectancy and SRL did not predict intention. The model explained 62.1% to 70.9% of endogenous variance and showed out-of-sample predictive relevance. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and full-collinearity diagnostics indicating possible common-method variance, the findings are interpreted as associations compatible with, but not establishing, the proposed mechanisms.

items.abstract_text: Digital competence among bank employees is an increasingly critical determinant of task efficiency in technology-driven financial service environments. In this study, a hybrid analytical approach is used that combines Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) with ten machine learning (ML) classifiers. The combination of these two approaches is designed to predict the Focused vs. Distracted attention status of bank employees based on multimodal behavioural and digital interaction features during task execution. The dataset included 1,000 observations of bank employees, capturing head orientation, facial expression, gaze direction, micro-movements, application usage, notification interruptions, and task completion time during digital work sessions. There was a marked imbalance in the class distribution with 91.2% of bank employees categorized as Distracted and 8.8% of bank employees categorized as Focused, which was consistent with the actual prevalence of digital distraction in professional banking environments. The LightGBM model performed best with all the classifiers, with an accuracy score of 98.9%, an AUC of 0.9998, and an F1 score of 0.989. Random Forest and XGBoost followed closely with an AUC of 0.9996 and 0.9995, respectively. The top 3 explainable features identified by SHAP analysis were Head Orientation, Facial Expression and Micro-Movements. The necessity analysis using the fsQCA method confirmed that forward gaze (consistency = 0.97), straight head posture (0.94) and neutral facial expression (0.99) are almost necessary conditions for focused attention. The results provide actionable insights for intelligent workforce management systems, adaptive digital workplace platforms, and real-time employee performance monitoring systems in banking and financial service organizations.
